transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jared (Redwood SE), Lina (Parcelly - Head of Platform), Omar (SRE), Priya (ML)

Summary:
Weekly POC check-in focused on a spike of intermittent 5xx and timeouts observed during customer synthetic peak tests. Discussed root cause hypotheses (cold k/v cache, request fanout, circuit breaker sensitivity, model switching), short-term mitigations (adaptive retries with jitter, client backoff, prioritized routing, warmup probe), and next steps for a targeted load test, data collection, and follow-up RCA.

Topics:
- Incident symptoms and timeline
- Retry and backoff tuning recommendations
- Rate limiting and circuit breaker thresholds
- KV cache warming and probe strategy
- Short-term fallback options (smaller model / lower context length)
- Observability gaps and log artifacts to collect

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um we saw the spike in 5xxs on monday when you did the end-to-end throughput replay, right? wanted to go through what we saw and outline a playbook.
[00:12] Lina: yeah thanks maya, that was our internal stress run, we pushed about 420 rps for short bursts, roughly three minutes, and then we started seeing timeouts and then a bunch of 502s come back.
[00:22] Omar: correct, most of the 5xxs were concentrated around 10:07–10:10 our time, latency for successful requests climbed too, some tails to 6s which violates the 2s SLO.
[00:33] Jared: quick context from the Redwood side — the run you did hit a hot-key pattern where a small percentage of prompts are long and cause big kv cache pressure which can blow up tail latency. Also if the probe/warmup didn't keep the tensor cache hot, the first few requests per session will be heavier.
[00:50] Priya: we did notice a subset of prompts that include long context (like the product catalog blobs) — i can share the prompt list after this.
[01:00] Maya: perfect. so the likely suspects: kv-cache cold starts, model memory contention under burst, and potentially rate-windowing interaction where the circuit breaker trips on backend worker queue growth. would you all be comfortable letting us run a focused test?
[01:18] Lina: yes, that's our ask. we want the load test to be as close to prod as possible — same prompt mix and same burst profile.
[01:25] Jared: ok plan — we'll run a 30 minute targeted test from our side in the staging environment with 3 phases: warmup with small sustained rps to prime kv cache, a ramp to the peak burst, and then a cool down. we'll capture traces, worker queue metrics, and the token-emit timelines.
[01:44] Omar: couple of things, can we get a list of headers/trace ids to filter in our logs? also our PD tags will help correlate.
[01:50] Maya: yes we'll include trace sample ids; jared will paste a filter snapshot into the shared slack channel after the run.
[01:57] [02:00] Jared: on retries — we recommend a client-side golden path: 1) immediate fast retry with small jitter only for idempotent calls, 2) exponential backoff after two fast retries, 3) clamp total retry budget per user to avoid thundering herd. also implement a 429 handling path separate from 5xx.
[02:22] Priya: curious on the preferred retry counts — we saw some clients doing up to 5 retries which made the backend queue worse.
[02:28] Jared: yeah, five is too many for bursty workloads. we recommend at most 2 fast retries (100–300ms jitter), then stop and surface failure. combine with a circuit breaker on server-side that opens when queue latency > X.
[02:43] Maya: and on the server side we can tune the circuit breaker thresholds — for your workload we suggest trimming the worker queue depth threshold and lowering the window length to detect spikes faster.
[02:52] Omar: do you have a suggestion for the numbers? we need concrete to push to our infra team.
[02:57] Jared: propose starting with queue depth threshold = 25, window = 10s, open for 30s, then half-open probe at 10% traffic. if you still see early tripping, we can reduce to depth 15. those are starting points not gospel.
[03:12] Lina: ok that seems reasonable.
[03:15] [03:18] Priya: what about fallback model options? maybe we can switch to a smaller quantized model when the heavy model shows high queue depth?
[03:24] Jared: yes — graceful fallback to a smaller model is part of the playbook. two key caveats: 1) you must accept lower quality or truncated context, 2) ensure routing supports safe fallback without violating data residency if using different infra. we can configure automatic fallback in the routing policy with a priority list: primary model -> quantized variant -> small model.
[03:47] Maya: also caching responses for repeated prompts can avoid repeat work — we noticed many of your prompts are deterministic. an additional layer is prefix caching for common system prompts.
[03:58] Omar: quick note — our security team prefers not to cache certain PII-rich prompts. how does Redwood handle cache encryption and purging?
[04:06] Jared: cache entries are ephemeral and optionally encrypted with KMS per-tenant when deployed on Dedicated/Private. we can share the cache lifecycle doc — will attach to follow-up.
[04:15] [04:18] Lina: regarding observability gaps — we had trouble correlating 502s with worker queues because some logs are sampled. can you increase sampling for the next run?
[04:27] Maya: yes, we'll do full trace sampling for the duration of the load test and share the full traces. we'll also include span breakdowns for tokenization, KV lookup, and forward pass.
[04:38] Priya: one more ask — can you include model-level token counts per request in the trace? that will help us tie long prompts to cost/laten cy.
[04:45] Jared: yes, we'll add token count metadata to the spans.
[04:48] [05:00] Omar: about rate limiting — we saw a few 429s earlier but mostly 502s. any guidance on how to configure client rate limits?
[05:07] Jared: two-tier approach: soft client-side rate limiter (leaky bucket) tuned to your steady-state rps, and server-side token bucket with short refill intervals for burst smoothing. avoid large single-burst leaky bucket sizes.
[05:22] Maya: additionally, set a per-route concurrency cap for heavy prompts. if you have a heavy prompt route, give it a lower concurrency limit and use a separate queue.
[05:32] Priya: that sounds like work on our side — we can create a separate route for catalog-embedding prompts.
[05:37] [06:00] Jared: also, you may want to try shortening context length for the top 2% of heavy prompts — drop non-critical history or summarize on the client to reduce token emission.
[06:12] Lina: ok good. what about a quick mitigation for today if this happens in prod?
[06:17] Maya: immediate steps: 1) flip to smaller model fallback via the routing policy if available, 2) temporarily lower concurrency caps for suspect routes, 3) push a client-side soft limiter or divert a portion of traffic to a canary region.
[06:32] Omar: in terms of rollback, how quick is rollback of a routing policy?
[06:35] Jared: routing changes are instant — but warmup matters: if fallback model is cold, you may see initial latency; so we recommend proactive warmup calls to the fallback model when you flip the policy.
[06:47] [07:00] Priya: will the warmup calls count toward my bill? we need to weigh cost.
[07:05] Maya: yes warmup is billable as normal token usage. we can help calculate a warmup budget vs the expected reduction in 5xx cost.
[07:14] Lina: speaking of cost, can you send the burst pricing addendum? we need delta between hosted bursts vs Dedicated reserved capacity.
[07:21] Maya: sure, i'll send a spreadsheet with baseline cost, estimated token units for your workload, and the Dedicated reserved capacity options.
[07:29] [08:00] Omar: during your run can you also enable extra server-side logs for queue length and GC pauses? we've suspected GC as a contributor.
[08:08] Jared: we'll enable additional runtime diagnostics — worker GC/alloc metrics and queue-frame histograms.
[08:16] Priya: do you have examples of adaptive backoff configs you use in other customers? a starting template would help.
[08:22] Jared: yes we'll drop a template in the shared doc — includes recommended jitter, max retries, and per-user retry budget.
[08:29] [09:00] Lina: how about SLA — if we move to Dedicated can we get a lower tail latency SLA?
[09:06] Maya: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and we can negotiate tighter SLOs as part of the reserved capacity contract, including priority routing and pre-warmed pools for your tenant. i'll outline options in the follow-up.
[09:17] Omar: timeline — we have a security review on friday, after that we'd like to decide whether to start a 2-week pilot on Dedicated if the mitigation looks promising.
[09:26] Maya: great. next steps recap: jared runs the load test with full tracing and increased sampling; omer shares console PD tags and incident timeline; priya shares prompt set and SLOs; maya sends pricing and docs.
[09:38] [10:00] Priya: quick call-out — a few transcriptions in our logs show k v cash instead of kv cache, just a heads up, some of the older export tools mangle acronyms.
[10:09] Jared: haha noted, we'll use consistent naming in the doc.
[10:15] Lina: any questions before we wrap?
[10:18] Omar: none from SRE.
[10:20] Priya: none.
[10:22] Maya: ok thanks all — we'll target the runs tomorrow morning and follow up with artifacts in slack + the shared drive.
[10:30] Lina: thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
